sections.content: Asheville, North Carolina has quietly become one of the hottest real estate markets in the Southeast. Tucked into the Blue Ridge Mountains, this mid-sized city draws retirees, remote workers, artists, and tourists in droves — and that demand fuels strong opportunities for investors. Whether you are looking for a fix-and-flip, a long-term rental, or your first wholesale deal, finding real estate deals in Asheville NC requires knowing the local landscape. If you are brand new to investing, start with our Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide before diving in. For everyone else, let's get into what makes Asheville tick — and how to find deals that actually pencil out.
Asheville NC Market Overview: Why Investors Are Paying Attention

Asheville sits in Buncombe County and has a population of around 95,000, but the greater metro area tops 470,000 residents. The city consistently ranks on national "best places to live" lists, thanks to its arts scene, outdoor recreation, craft beer culture, and mild four-season climate. Tourism is a major economic driver — Asheville hosted over 11 million visitors in 2023 — which keeps short-term rental demand very high. At the same time, a steady inflow of remote workers and retirees from pricier markets like Miami, New York, and Washington D.C. has pushed home prices upward over the past five years. Unemployment in the Asheville metro typically runs below 4%, and the local economy benefits from healthcare, hospitality, and a growing tech sector. In short, this is a market with real, sustained demand — not just hype.
Average Home Prices in Asheville NC

As of mid-2024, the median home price in Asheville proper sits around $450,000 — a figure that has climbed roughly 55% since 2019. However, prices vary dramatically by neighborhood and property type. Older ranch-style homes and bungalows in working-class areas can still be found in the $200,000–$280,000 range, which is where most wholesale and flip opportunities live. Higher-end zip codes like West Asheville and the River Arts District routinely see sales above $550,000. For investors, the key is understanding after-repair value (ARV) for each submarket. Use our free ARV Calculator to quickly estimate post-renovation value before you make an offer — it can save you from overpaying on a deal that looks attractive on the surface.
Best Neighborhoods for Real Estate Investors in Asheville

Not every corner of Asheville offers equal opportunity. Investors who know where to focus will find better margins, faster exits, and stronger rental income. Here are the top areas to explore on our Asheville NC market page.

items: West Asheville: A hip, walkable neighborhood with strong short-term rental demand and solid appreciation. Flips here target buyers willing to pay a premium for character homes close to restaurants and nightlife.

South Asheville: More suburban feel with newer construction, good schools, and strong long-term rental demand from families and healthcare workers. Lower crime makes it attractive for buy-and-hold investors.

East Asheville: One of the more affordable entry points in the city. Older housing stock means more distressed properties and wholesale opportunities. Values are rising as buyers get priced out of West Asheville.
River Arts District (RAD): Undergoing rapid gentrification. Mixed-use and short-term rental plays are popular here. Watch for zoning restrictions before assuming short-term rental approval.
Swannanoa & Black Mountain: Suburban communities just east of Asheville proper. More affordable price points ($180,000–$300,000) with strong rental demand and growing investor interest.
North Asheville: Higher price points near UNCA (UNC Asheville). Student rental demand is consistent, and the area attracts long-term renters who work in the medical district.

sections.content: Types of Real Estate Deals Available in Asheville
Wholesale Deals

Wholesaling in Asheville is competitive but absolutely viable. The best wholesale opportunities are distressed properties — inherited homes, deferred-maintenance ranches, and properties owned by out-of-state landlords ready to exit. Motivated sellers in East Asheville, Swannanoa, and the older pockets of North Asheville are where many wholesalers focus. Assignment fees in the $10,000–$25,000 range are common on deals that come in at 65–70% of ARV minus repairs. If you are new to the process, read our guide on Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners to understand how to structure contracts and find buyers fast.
Fix-and-Flip

Asheville's rising home prices create favorable conditions for flippers — as long as you buy right. A typical flip in East Asheville might involve a 3-bedroom, 1-bath home purchased at $195,000, renovated for $55,000, and sold at $315,000, yielding a gross profit of around $65,000 before holding costs, financing, and agent fees. Always run your numbers before committing. Our free Deal Calculator lets you model renovation budgets, financing costs, and profit projections in seconds. The biggest mistake flippers make in Asheville is underestimating rehab costs — older homes often have knob-and-tube wiring, cast iron plumbing, and foundation issues that add up quickly.
Long-Term Rentals

Average rents in Asheville run $1,400–$1,800 per month for a two-bedroom unit and $1,800–$2,400 for a three-bedroom. Healthcare workers at Mission Hospital, students at UNCA, and service industry employees all fuel consistent rental demand. The challenge is achieving positive cash flow given current purchase prices. Investors who buy in the $220,000–$280,000 range in South or East Asheville can still find deals that cash flow $300–$600 per month after PITI and property management.
Short-Term Rentals (STRs)

Asheville is one of the top STR markets in the Southeast, with average Airbnb revenue of $35,000–$55,000 per year for well-located properties. However, the city has implemented STR licensing regulations, and some zones restrict or prohibit short-term rentals. Always verify zoning and licensing requirements with Buncombe County and the City of Asheville before purchasing with STR income in mind.
In a market like Asheville, the investors who win aren't the ones chasing listed properties — they're the ones who find motivated sellers before the property ever hits the MLS.
How to Find Off-Market Deals in Asheville

Listed properties in Asheville rarely offer the margins investors need. The real opportunities are off-market — properties where the seller has a reason to move quickly and quietly. Direct mail campaigns targeting absentee owners, probate leads, and tax-delinquent properties in Buncombe County are proven strategies. Driving for dollars in East Asheville and Swannanoa can surface deals that never touch the MLS. For a full breakdown of off-market sourcing strategies, check out our guide on How to Find Off-Market Real Estate Deals. Once you have a lead, it is equally important to analyze it properly — our guide on How to Analyze Real Estate Deals Like a Pro walks you through the exact process.

Pro Tip: Pull the Buncombe County tax records for properties with out-of-state mailing addresses in zip codes 28801, 28803, and 28805. Absentee owners in East and South Asheville are among the most motivated sellers in the market. A simple postcard campaign to 500 of these owners can generate 3–5 serious leads per month.
Asheville Real Estate Market Trends to Watch in 2024

items: Price softening in the luxury segment: Homes above $700,000 are sitting longer as mortgage rates keep move-up buyers on the sideline. This creates negotiating leverage at the high end.
Rising insurance costs: Western NC has seen homeowner insurance premiums climb 20–30% in 2023–2024 due to storm and flood risk. Factor this into your rental and flip pro formas.

Infrastructure growth: Asheville's airport (AVL) is expanding, and new hotel and mixed-use developments are planned for the River Arts District and downtown. These projects tend to lift surrounding property values.
STR regulatory pressure: City Council has debated tightening short-term rental rules. Monitor local zoning updates closely if STR income is part of your strategy.
Inventory remains tight: Active listings in Buncombe County typically run 30–40% below pre-pandemic norms, which supports pricing but makes finding deals harder through conventional channels.

sections.content: Practical Tips for Out-of-State Investors

Investing remotely in Asheville is absolutely doable, but it requires building the right team on the ground. Start by connecting with a local investor-friendly real estate agent who understands ARV, repair estimates, and deal structure — not just retail sales. Next, build relationships with a general contractor and a property manager before you close your first deal. Asheville has a tight contractor market, and lead times for renovation work can run 6–10 weeks. Budget for that in your holding cost calculations. Join the local REIA (Real Estate Investors Association) chapter and connect with wholesalers who have active deal flow. Finally, visit the market in person at least once before committing capital — Asheville's neighborhoods are very different from each other, and boots-on-the-ground knowledge is irreplaceable.

Pro Tip: When evaluating a property remotely, request a detailed video walkthrough that includes the basement, attic, electrical panel, and HVAC system. These are the four biggest cost surprises in older Asheville homes. Pair the video with a local inspector's report before making any offer.
